title: Rays and Gaps: Almost-All Goldbach Theorems for Consecutive and Shifted Primes
content: For \( q=2^k \) and \( \gcd(a,q)=1 \) let \( R_{a,q}(N) = \sum_{p_1+p_2=N,\ p_1\equiv a \pmod{q}} (\log p_1)(\log p_2) \) be the restricted weighted Goldbach sum, with candidate main term\( M_{a,q}(N)=2C_2/\varphi(q)\mathfrak{S}(N)N \) and exceptional set \( \mathcal{E}_{a,q}(X)=\{N\le X\text{ even: }R_{a,q}(N)=0\} \). Writing \( p_n \) for the \( n \)-th prime, \( g_n=p_{n+1}-p_n \) and \( N_n=p_n+p_{n+1} \), we prove an elementary transfer principle: if \( f \)maps a set of indices injectively (or with bounded multiplicity) into the even integers with at most linear growth, then the number of indices \( n\le X \) with \( R_{a,q}(f(n))=0 \) is at most a bounded multiple of \( \#\mathcal{E}_{a,q}(\kappa X) \). Consequences are uniform in the residue class (“ray”) modulo \( q \), and cover \( N_n=p_n+p_{n+1},\,p_n+p_{n+k} \) and the shifted primes \( p+h\ \) with \( h \) odd. A mean-value lemma of Tolev gives \( \#\mathcal{E}_{a,q}(X)\ll_{q,A}X(\log X)^{-A} \) for every \( A>0 \) when \( q=2^k \), and hence each of these sets of even integers has a restricted Goldbach representation for almost all primes in every ray, with a saving of every power of \( \log X \). We record which of these representations are trivial (a summand equal to \( p_n \) or \( p_{n+1} \)) and which are not. For a modulus q with an odd prime factor \( \ell \) we prove that \( N_n\equiv a\pmod{\ell} \) is equivalent to a condition on the pair of rays of pn and pn+1, that \( R_{a,q}(N_n)=O(\log N_n) \) on that set, and, by a theorem of Shiu, that this set is infinite; for q=3 we verify exactly that \( R_{a,q}(N_n)=0 \) if and only if \( N_n\equiv 1\pmod{3} \) and \( N_n-3 \) is composite. The digit-repulsion bias of Lemke Oliver and Soundararajan is documented on 5,761,451 consecutive pairs below 108, together with the dependence of the mean gap on the ray of origin and a fit of the cumulative admissibility function. For q=5 the same equivalence holds with three small exceptions. We also compare the mod-3 joint frequencies of consecutive primes with the Lemke Oliver–Soundararajan prediction at three scales. Next we show that the relative second moment of \( R_{a,q}(N)-M_{a,q}(N) \) depends on \( N\bmod q \) through the symmetry \( p_1\leftrightarrow p_2 \): for \( N\equiv 2a\pmod{q} \) the variance ratio is 2.0 to 2.1 for q=8,16,32, all within about one standard error of \( 2 \). Along Nn this class effect, together with the residues of Nn modulo 3 and 5, predicts the second moment by ray of pn to within 3% overall, and predicts the ray differences (which are significant at z=7 to 9) to within about two standard errors. Applied unchanged at q=16, with the recipe fixed in advance, it predicts the level to 2%, the spread among the eight rays to 2%, and the pattern across rays with correlation 0.96, with a residual over-prediction of 2% to 3% at all four pairs \( (q,a) \) tested, which shrinks to about 1% when the classes modulo 7 and 11 are added (exploratory). In a temporal split of the primes below 108, the last ray predicts the next ray with accuracy 0.311 against 0.25 (at most 0.316 with more rays), while the rays of the past explain at most 0.19% of the variance of the normalised gap. Every statement carries an explicit status label.
